### Example 1 · Page 104

$z=\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}$. Find the exact value of:

**(a)** $z^6$;

**(b)** $\dfrac1{z^2}$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Using de Moivre's theorem, $(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^n=\cos n\theta+\mathrm i\sin n\theta$.

**(a)**

$$
z^6=\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^6
=\cos\frac{6\pi}{4}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{6\pi}{4}
=\cos\frac{3\pi}{2}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}
=\boxed{-\mathrm i}.
$$

**(b)**

$$
\frac1{z^2}=z^{-2}
=\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)^{-2}
=\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)+\mathrm i\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)
=\boxed{-\mathrm i}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="cn-p2-example-1"> Completed</label>
:::

### Example 2 · Page 108

**(a)** Find the eighth roots of unity.

**(b)** Show that they can all be written as powers of $\dfrac{\mathrm i-1}{\sqrt2}$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

**(a)** The roots are equally spaced around the unit circle. The angle between adjacent roots is

$$
\frac{2\pi}{8}=\frac{\pi}{4}.
$$

Four of the roots are $1$, $-1$, $\mathrm i$ and $-\mathrm i$. The other four are

$$
\pm\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{4}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{\pi}{4}\right)
=\pm\frac{1+\mathrm i}{\sqrt2},
$$

and

$$
\pm\left(\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)
=\pm\frac{-1+\mathrm i}{\sqrt2}.
$$

So the eighth roots of unity are

$$
\boxed{\pm1,\ \pm\mathrm i,\ \pm\frac{1+\mathrm i}{\sqrt2},\ \pm\frac{-1+\mathrm i}{\sqrt2}}.
$$

**(b)** Let

$$
w=\frac{\mathrm i-1}{\sqrt2}=\cos\frac{3\pi}{4}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{3\pi}{4}.
$$

Then $w=e^{\mathrm i3\pi/4}$, so the powers $w^0,w^1,w^2,\dots,w^7$ are

$$
1,\ w,\ w^2,\ w^3,\ w^4,\ w^5,\ w^6,\ w^7,
$$

which are the points $e^{\mathrm i 3k\pi/4}$ for $k=0,1,\dots,7$. These are exactly the eight equally spaced roots found in part (a).

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="cn-p2-example-2"> Completed</label>
:::

### Example 3 · Page 109

**(a)** Find the cube roots of $8$.

**(b)** Find the cube roots of $8\mathrm i$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

**(a)** Let $z=r(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)$. Then $z^3=r^3(\cos3\theta+\mathrm i\sin3\theta)=8$. Hence $r^3=8$, so $r=2$, and $\cos3\theta=1$, $\sin3\theta=0$, so $3\theta$ is a multiple of $2\pi$:

$$
3\theta=0,\ 2\pi,\ 4\pi,\ 6\pi,\dots
$$

The three distinct values of $\theta$ are $0$, $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ and $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$. Hence the cube roots of $8$ are

$$
\boxed{2,\quad
2\left(\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}\right),\quad
2\left(\cos\frac{4\pi}{3}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)}.
$$

**(b)** Now $z^3=8\mathrm i$, so $r=2$ and

$$
\cos3\theta+\mathrm i\sin3\theta=\mathrm i=\cos\frac{\pi}{2}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Thus $3\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+2k\pi$, giving $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\dfrac{5\pi}{6},\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$. The cube roots of $8\mathrm i$ are

$$
\boxed{
2\left(\cos\frac{\pi}{6}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{\pi}{6}\right),\quad
2\left(\cos\frac{5\pi}{6}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{5\pi}{6}\right),\quad
2\left(\cos\frac{3\pi}{2}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{3\pi}{2}\right)=-2\mathrm i
}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="cn-p2-example-3"> Completed</label>
:::

### Example 4 · Page 111

**(a)** Use de Moivre's theorem to prove that

$$
\cos3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta.
$$

**(b)** Solve the equation $\cos3\theta+\cos\theta=0$ for $0\leqslant\theta<2\pi$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

**(a)** By de Moivre's theorem,

$$
(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^3=\cos3\theta+\mathrm i\sin3\theta.
$$

Expanding the left-hand side,

$$
(\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta)^3
=\cos^3\theta+3\mathrm i\cos^2\theta\sin\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta-\mathrm i\sin^3\theta.
$$

Taking real parts,

$$
\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta.
$$

Using $\sin^2\theta=1-\cos^2\theta$,

$$
\cos3\theta=\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta(1-\cos^2\theta)
=\boxed{4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta}.
$$

**(b)** Using part (a),

$$
\cos3\theta+\cos\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta+\cos\theta
=2\cos\theta(2\cos^2\theta-1)=0.
$$

So $\cos\theta=0$ or $\cos^2\theta=\dfrac12$. Hence

$$
\boxed{\theta=\frac{\pi}{2},\ \frac{3\pi}{2},\ \frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{3\pi}{4},\ \frac{5\pi}{4},\ \frac{7\pi}{4}}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="cn-p2-example-4"> Completed</label>
:::

### Example 5 · Page 113

**(a)** Show that

$$
\sin^3\theta=\frac14(3\sin\theta-\sin3\theta).
$$

**(b)** Hence find $\displaystyle\int\sin^3\theta\,\mathrm d\theta$.

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

**(a)** Let $z=\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta$. Then

$$
z-z^{-1}=2\mathrm i\sin\theta.
$$

Cubing,

$$
(2\mathrm i\sin\theta)^3=(z-z^{-1})^3
=z^3-3z+3z^{-1}-z^{-3}.
$$

Using $z^n+z^{-n}=2\cos n\theta$ and $z^n-z^{-n}=2\mathrm i\sin n\theta$,

$$
(z-z^{-1})^3=(z^3-z^{-3})-3(z-z^{-1})
=2\mathrm i\sin3\theta-6\mathrm i\sin\theta.
$$

Hence

$$
-8\mathrm i\sin^3\theta=2\mathrm i\sin3\theta-6\mathrm i\sin\theta,
$$

so

$$
\boxed{\sin^3\theta=\frac14(3\sin\theta-\sin3\theta)}.
$$

**(b)**

$$
\int\sin^3\theta\,\mathrm d\theta
=\frac14\int(3\sin\theta-\sin3\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta
=\boxed{-\frac34\cos\theta+\frac1{12}\cos3\theta+C}.
$$

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="cn-p2-example-5"> Completed</label>
:::

### Example 6 · Page 117

Show that

$$
\sum_{r=1}^{4}\cos r\theta=\frac{\sin2\theta\,\cos\frac{5\theta}{2}}{\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}.
$$

<details class="answer-panel"><summary>Show solution</summary>

Let $z=\cos\theta+\mathrm i\sin\theta$ and write

$$
C+\mathrm iS=z+z^2+z^3+z^4.
$$

Then the real part $C=\sum_{r=1}^4\cos r\theta$. The sum is a geometric series:

$$
z+z^2+z^3+z^4=\frac{z(z^4-1)}{z-1}.
$$

Now

$$
z^4-1=\cos4\theta+\mathrm i\sin4\theta-1
=-2\sin^22\theta+2\mathrm i\sin2\theta\cos2\theta
=2\mathrm i\sin2\theta(\cos2\theta+\mathrm i\sin2\theta)
=2\mathrm i z^2\sin2\theta,
$$

and

$$
z-1=\cos\theta-1+\mathrm i\sin\theta
=-2\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2}+2\mathrm i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2}
=2\mathrm i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\left(\cos\frac{\theta}{2}+\mathrm i\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\right)
=2\mathrm i z^{1/2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}.
$$

Therefore

$$
C+\mathrm iS
=\frac{z\cdot2\mathrm i z^2\sin2\theta}{2\mathrm i z^{1/2}\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}
=z^{5/2}\frac{\sin2\theta}{\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}.
$$

Taking real parts,

$$
\boxed{\sum_{r=1}^{4}\cos r\theta
=\frac{\sin2\theta\,\cos\frac{5\theta}{2}}{\sin\frac{\theta}{2}}}.
$$

This is the $C+\mathrm iS$ method.

</details>
<label class="done-toggle"><input type="checkbox" data-progress="cn-p2-example-6"> Completed</label>
:::
